--- title: Declock description: > Introducing Declock, a timekeeping system that displays time in decimal days without the need for hours, minutes, or seconds. image: /asset/daywide.svg url: https://maptv.github.io/dec/time decdate: 2026+242 path: /dec/time slug: time aliases: - /time - /dt engine: knitr draft: true --- ::: {.timenav} ::: # Declock {#declock .hiddenheading} My website provides many examples of the [Quarto](https://quarto.org) publishing and the [Dec](/dec) measurement systems in action. I leverage Quarto support for the [Observable](https://observablehq.com/) data analysis and visualization system to create animated and interactive graphics like the [bar📊charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_chart) clocks🕓, [solar☀️terminator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminator_%28solar%29#:~:text=a%20moving%20line%20that%20divides%20the%20daylit%20side%20and%20the%20dark%20night%20side%20of%20a%20planetary%20body) map🗺, [Earth🌍orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_orbit) diagram, and [daylight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight#:~:text=the%20combination%20of%20all%20direct%20and%20indirect%20sunlight%20during%20the%20daytime) [area chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_chart#:~:text=The%20area%20between%20axis%20and%20line%20are%20commonly%20emphasized%20with%20colors) below. ::: {.column-margin .clocks #onlymargin .posneg} \${posclock}\${negclock} ::: Dec times are measured in [fractional days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#Fractional_days:~:text=a%20decimal%20fraction%20of%20a%20day), often using [metric prefixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_prefix#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20that%20precedes%20a%20basic%20unit%20of%20measure%20to%20indicate%20a%20multiple%20or%20submultiple%20of%20the%20unit) like [deci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deci-#:~:text=a%20decimal%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20tenth), [centi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centi-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20hundredth), or [milli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milli-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20thousandth). The top, middle, and bottom bars indicate the [decidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#:~:text=dividing%20the%20day%20into%2010%20decidays){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"}, [millidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_time#:~:text=1.44%20minutes%2C%20or%2086.4%20seconds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a day"}, and [centimillidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#:~:text=which%20would%20be-,1/100%2C000%20day,-%2C%20or%20864%20milliseconds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundred thousandths of a day"}, respectively, of the time since the start, [+\${decTime}]{.point1}, or until the end, [-\${decTimeN}]{.point0}, of the day in the Dec [time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone#:~:text=an%20area%20which%20observes%20a%20uniform%20standard%20time), \${decZoneHsl}, at the location of the red⭕️circle on the map beneath the bars. To rotate the globe🌐in the Earth🌏orbit diagram, drag the red circle horizontally↔️or slide the red🔴dot on the daylight area chart vertically↕. The red circle's vertical position determines the yearly daylight pattern visualized by the area chart. {#sec-ada .hiddenheading} The red line indicates a "day of year" ([doy](#doy){#dayofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}): \${selDateHsl}, which identifies a day in a year like a [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) month and "day of month" ([dom](#dom){#dayofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}). The red dot denotes a "time of day" ([tod](#tod){#timeofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}): \${selTimeDay}, which specifies a point in a day like an "hour minute second" ([hms](#hms){#hourminutesecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"}) triplet. Together, a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can form an "annual day aggregate" ([ada](#ada){#annualdayaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}): \${selDateHsl1} + \${selTimeDay1} ÷ 1000 = \${selDateHsl2}.\${selTimeDay2}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup00} $$ \begin{split} \text{doy} &= \lfloor\text{ada}\rfloor \\ &= \text{ada} - \text{tod} \end{split} $$ {#eq-ada} ::: As their names suggest, [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} and [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"} are measured in days. The [measurement unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_measurement#:~:text=a%20definite%20magnitude%20of%20a%20quantity) of a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can be a day or a [submultiple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_%28mathematics%29#Submultiple:~:text=of%20%22a%20being-,a%20unit%20fraction,-of%20b%22%20) of a day with a metric prefix. By changing how a decimal [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is measured, we can shift its [decimal separator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_separator#:~:text=a%20symbol%20that%20separates%20the%20integer%20part%20from%20the%20fractional%20part%20of%20a%20number) or turn it into an integer. The [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} along the y-axis of the area chart are integers because they have three digits and are measured in [millidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a day"}. # Epochal day aggregate (eda) {#sec-eda .hiddenheading} To obtain a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}, we can [keep the remainder after dividing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) by one to isolate the [decimal part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part#:~:text=the%20excess%20beyond%20that%20number%27s%20integer%20part) of the [quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient#:~:text=a%20quantity%20produced%20by%20the%20division%20of%20two%20numbers): \${zeroDotyHsl}.\${zeroTimeHsl0} [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 = [0]{.color0}.\${zeroTimeHsl1}. We can use this same approach to separate a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from an "epochal day aggregate" ([eda](#eda){#epochaldayaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"}): \${zeroDoteHsl}.\${zeroTimeHsl2} mod 1 = [0]{.color0}.\${zeroTimeHsl3}. The current [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"} tells us how many days have passed since the Dec [epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoch#:~:text=an%20instant%20in%20time%20chosen%20as%20the%20origin%20of%20a%20particular%20calendar%20era): Year [0]{.color0} Day [0]{.color0} [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [0]{.color0}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup01} $$\begin{split} \text{tod} &= \text{ada} \bmod 1 \\ &= \text{eda} \bmod 1 \end{split}$$ {#eq-tod} ::: ## UNIX time equation {#sec-ute .unnumbered .hiddenheading} Similarly, [UNIX time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=the%20number%20of%20non%2Dleap%20seconds%20that%20have%20elapsed%20since%2000%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970%2C%20the%20Unix%20epoch) tallies the seconds since the [UNIX epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=00%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970), which is exactly 719468 days after the Dec epoch. To get the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in Zone [0]{.color0}, the Dec time zone that is in between the two leftmost vertical lines on the map, we can divide UNIX time by the [number of seconds in a day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#:~:text=average%2C%20this%20is-,24%20hours%20(86%2C400%20seconds),-.%20As%20a%20day) and then keep the remainder after dividing the resulting days by 1 as in @eq-unixtod. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup02} $$\text{tod} = \text{unix} \div 86400 \bmod 1$$ {#eq-unixtod} ::: ## Julian date equation {#sec-jde .unnumbered .hiddenheading} [Julian dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=the%20Julian%20day%20number%20plus%20the%20fraction%20of%20a%20day%20since%20the%20preceding%20noon) track the days since the beginning of the [Julian period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=a%20chronological%20interval%20of%207980%C2%A0years%2C%20derived%20from%20three%20multi%2Dyear%20cycles:%20the%20Indiction%2C%20Solar%2C%20and%20Lunar%20cycles) and thus are akin to [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregates"}. We can produce a Zone [5]{.color5} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [Julian date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=the%20Julian%20day%20number%20plus%20the%20fraction%20of%20a%20day%20since%20the%20preceding%20noon) simply by keeping the remainder after dividing by one. If we want a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} instead, we should add [5]{.color5} [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to the Julian date, divide the sum by one, and then keep the remainder as in @eq-juliantod below. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup03} $$\text{tod} = (\text{julian} + 0.5) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-juliantod} ::: # Hour minute second {#sec-hms .hiddenheading} We can also obtain a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time#:~:text=the%20primary%20time%20standard%20globally%20used%20to%20regulate%20clocks%20and%20time) ([UTC](#utc){#coordinateduniversaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet by summing its components after converting them to fractional days, as shown in the equation below. The [computer programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programming#:~:text=the%20composition%20of%20sequences%20of%20instructions%2C%20called%20programs%2C%20that%20computers%20can%20follow%20to%20perform%20tasks) code in the [tabset panel](https://quarto.org/docs/interactive/layout.html#tabset-panel) beneath the equation compares [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} derived from [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} and UNIX time as Quarto was [rendering](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/rstudio.html#rendering:~:text=When%20rendering%2C%20Quarto%20generates%20a%20new%20file%20that%20contains%20selected%20text%2C%20code%2C%20and%20results) this webpage. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup04} $$\text{tod} = \dfrac{\text{hour}}{24} + \dfrac{\text{minute}}{1440} + \dfrac{\text{second}}{86400}$$ {#eq-hmstod} ::: :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Julia ::: {.cell} ```{.julia .cell-code} using Dates hms = now(UTC) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2026-10-30T14:47:26.076 ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} hour(hms) / 24 + minute(hms) / 1440 + second(hms) / 86400 + millisecond(hms) / 864e5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.6162740277777777 ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} datetime2unix(hms) / 86400 % 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.616274027775944 ``` ::: ::: ### Observable JavaScript ```{ojs} hms = new Date(); hms.getUTCHours() / 24 + hms.getUTCMinutes() / 1440 + hms.getUTCSeconds() / 86400 + hms.getUTCMilliseconds() / 864e5; hms.getTime() / 864e5 % 1; ``` ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from datetime import datetime, timezone hms = datetime.now(timezone.utc) hms.hour / 24 + \ hms.minute / 1440 + \ hms.second / 86400 + \ hms.microsecond / 864e8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.6162818051388889 ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} hms.timestamp() / 86400 % 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.6162818051379872 ``` ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hms <- as.POSIXlt(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC") hms$hour / 24 + hms$min / 1440 + hms$sec / 86400 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.616282 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (as.numeric(as.POSIXct(hms)) / 86400) %% 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.616282 ``` ::: ::: ::: Equations -@eq-dsa to -@eq-som below convert UNIX time or a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into the three components of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet: the "hour of day" ([hod](#hod){#hourofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"}), "minute of hour" ([moh](#moh){#minuteofhour .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="minute of hour"}), and "second of minute" ([som](#som){#secondofminute .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second of minute"}), using a "daily second aggregate" ([dsa](#dsa){#dailysecondaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daily second aggregate"}) and "hourly second aggregate" ([hsa](#hsa){#hourlysecondaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hourly second aggregate"}). While both count seconds, [dsa](#dsa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daily second aggregates"} start at midnight ([Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [0]{.color0}) and [hsa](#hsa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hourly second aggregates"} begin at the [top of the hour](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/top_of_the_hour). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup05} $$\begin{split} \text{dsa} & = \text{tod} \ast 86400 \\ & = \text{unix} \bmod 86400 \end{split} $$ {#eq-dsa} $$ \text{hsa} = \text{dsa} \bmod 3600 $$ {#eq-hsa} $$ \text{hod} = \lfloor \text{dsa} \div 3600 \rfloor $$ {#eq-hod} $$ \text{moh} = \lfloor \text{hsa} \div 60 \rfloor $$ {#eq-moh} $$ \text{som} = \lfloor \text{hsa} \bmod 60 \rfloor $$ {#eq-som} ::: :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Julia ::: {.cell} ```{.julia .cell-code} using Dates dsa = datetime2unix(now(UTC)) / 86400 % 1 * 86400 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 53246.80799993221 ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} hsa = dsa % 3600 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2846.807999932207 ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} map(x -> floor(Int, x), (dsa / 3600, hsa / 60, hsa % 60)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (14, 47, 26) ``` ::: ::: ### Observable JavaScript ```{ojs} dsa = Date.now() / 864e5 % 1 * 86400; hsa = dsa % 3600; [dsa / 3600, hsa / 60, hsa % 60].map(Math.floor) ``` ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from datetime import datetime, timezone dsa = datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp() / 86400 % 1 * 86400 hsa = dsa % 3600 tuple(map(int, [dsa // 3600, hsa // 60, hsa % 60 // 1])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (14, 47, 26) ``` ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dsa <- (as.numeric(as.POSIXct(Sys.time())) / 86400) %% 1 * 86400 hsa <- dsa %% 3600 sapply(c(dsa %/% 3600, hsa %/% 60, hsa %% 60), as.integer) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 14 47 26 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Universal time offset {#sec-uto .hiddenheading} The [Global Positioning System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System#:~:text=a%20satellite%2Dbased%20hyperbolic%20navigation%20system), [BeiDou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BeiDou#:~:text=a%20satellite%2Dbased%20radio%20navigation%20system), and [Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_(satellite_navigation)#:~:text=a%20global%20navigation%20satellite%20system%20(GNSS)%20created%20by%20the%20European%20Union) [global navigation satellite systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_navigation#:~:text=a%20satellite%20navigation%20system%20with%20global%20coverage) along with most --- if not all --- [programming languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_language#:~:text=a%20system%20of%20notation%20for%20writing%20source%20code%20such%20as%20used%20to%20produce%20a%20computer%20program) do not account for [leap seconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=one%2Dsecond%20adjustment), which appears to be for the best given that leap seconds [can cause problems](https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/leap-seconds-faqs#:~:text=detriments%20to%20adding%20leap%20seconds) and will be abolished no later than [2027]{.color27by100}+[081]{.color081by366} according to the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures#:~:text=an%20intergovernmental%20organisation%20(IGO)%2C%20through%20which%20its%2067%20member%2Dstates%20act%20on%20measurement%20standards). On or before the deadline to abolish leap seconds, the tolerance for disagreement between [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} and [Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Time#Versions:~:text=a%20time%20standard%20based%20on%20Earth%27s%20rotation) ([UT](#ut){#universaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"}) will increase from [1 Dec second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=to%20ensure%20that%20the%20difference%20between%20the%20UTC%20and%20UT1%20readings%20will%20never%20exceed%200.9%20seconds) ([s](#s){#second .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}) to 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}. Since [1972]{.color72by100}+[122]{.color122by365}, only [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=27%20leap%20seconds%20have%20been%20added%20to%20UTC) leap seconds have been inserted, which is 0.75% of 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, and at this rate it will take over five millennia for the disparity between [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} and [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to reach 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}. Instead of leap seconds, Dec matches [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} using a "[universal time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Time#:~:text=a%20time%20standard%20based%20on%20Earth%27s%20rotation) [offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC_offset#:~:text=the%20difference%20in%20hours%20and%20minutes%20between%20Coordinated%20Universal%20Time%20(UTC)%20and%20the%20standard%20time%20at%20a%20particular%20place)" ([uto](#uto){#universaltimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"}). With the [leap second insertion dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=Announced%20leap%20seconds%20to%20date) provided by the [International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Earth_Rotation_and_Reference_Systems_Service#:~:text=the%20body%20responsible%20for%20maintaining%20global%20time%20and%20reference%20frame%20standards), we can approximate the [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"} that yields [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} when added to the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} on the [Dec date](/dec/date) chosen by the [range](https://observablehq.com/framework/inputs/range)🎚️inputs below: \${leapCountHsl} ÷ 8640 = \${leapSdecHsl}\${leapSb24hsl} ÷ 90000 = \${leapTzoHsl0}. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: dateinput //| class: slider viewof leapSecondYear = Inputs.range([1970, 2020], {label: "Year", value: 1995, step: 1}) viewof leapSecondDate = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day", value: 182, step: 1}) ``` # Second interval difference {#sec-sid .hiddenheading} The equation above divides leap seconds by the number of [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#:~:text=the%20world%27s%20most%20widely%20used%20system%20of%20measurement) ([SI](#si){#internationalsystemofunits .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"}) seconds ([sis](#sis){#sisecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"}) or Dec [deciseconds]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a second"} ([ds](#ds){#decisecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}) in a [deciday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a day"} ([dd](#dd){#deciday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"}): 8640 [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} = 90000 [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"} = 1 [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"}. To avoid [repeating decimals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=the%20same%20sequence%20of%20digits%20is%20repeated%20forever) when turning [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} into [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}, we can put a Dec [quadravigesimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#:~:text=24-,Quadravigesimal,-%5B48%5D) ([base24]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadravigesimal"}) digit in place of the ones digit and decimal part of the [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}: \${leapSdecHsl1}\${leapSb24hsl1} = \${leapSdecHsl2} × 10 + \${leapSsidHsl} ÷ 2.4. Known as a "second interval difference" ([sid](#sid){#secondintervaldifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval difference"}), the [base24]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadravigesimal"} ([b24](#b24){#base24 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}) character at the end of \${leapSdecHsl3}\${leapSb24hsl2} is a letter of the [Greek alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_alphabet#:~:text=the%20writing%20system%20used%20for%20the%20Greek%20language). To display [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} in [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}, we can concatenate the integer part of the [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} we obtain from @eq-sis with the [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} representation of the [sid](#sid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval difference"} we get from @eq-sid. The table beneath these equations lists [base10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal#:~:text=a%20numeral%20system%20that%20uses%20ten%20as%20its%20radix%20%28base%29) ([b10](#b10){#base10 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}) and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} equivalents. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup06} $$ \text{s} = Like any base that is a multiple of 30, the combination of [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} and [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} is able to express any fraction whose denominator has no prime factors other than 2, 3, and 5 as a terminating decimal. and thus can handle not only the halves and thirds that bases which are multiples of 12, such as [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}, can end but also the fifths and tenths that those bases turn into repeating decimals. In short, [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} and [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} can do everything that [base30]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="trigesimal"}, [base60]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="sexagesimal"}, or [base360]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="trecentosexagesimal"} can do, albeit not always as succinctly, with only the ten decimal digits and nine astronomical symbols instead of 30, 60, or 360 different digits. [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} is the perfect complement to [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, because it adds only the missing prime factor, 3, and each [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit takes care of two factors of 3. Any [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digit from 1 to 8 that repeats forever can be replaced by one of the eight nonzero [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digits, [☿]{.color1by9 .mono} to [♆]{.color8by9 .mono}, because each [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit is worth the matching [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digit repeated forever: 1/3 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"} = 0.333… [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} = 0.[♁]{.color3by9 .mono} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and 1/6 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"} = 0.1666… [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} = 0.1[♄]{.color6by9 .mono} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. No [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit is needed for the other two [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, because a repeating 0 already terminates and [0.999…](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0.999...) is the same as 1. In the unit of its slot, a [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit is worth 10/9 of its value, never more than 0.89 above it, so it reads almost like a decimal digit, whereas [ω]{.color23by24 .mono} is worth 9.58. Since [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digits are astronomical symbols instead of numerals, we can always tell them apart from [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, which never change their meaning, unlike in [base12]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="duodecimal"}, where "10" means twelve. ## Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) {#sec-utc .hiddenheading} There are 12 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that become a terminating decimals after being converted from hours to days and therefore could be displayed in either [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} or [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Although it has only ten time zones, Dec can match the time in any [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with one or two non-negative [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. There are 27 UTC offsets that require only one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit and 11 that need two [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. Out of the [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets) [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, 14 are negative (<[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) and 24 are non-negative (≥[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}). The [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with [the most negative offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9212:00#:~:text=a%20nautical%20time%20zone%20comprising%20the%20high%20seas%20between%20180%C2%B0%20and%20172%C2%B030%E2%80%B2W%20longitude) is completely uninhabited. The bar chart below visualizes [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) data from 2020 regarding the population of each [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone. The vast majority of all people live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with ≥[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: timezonepoptoggles //| class: togs // https://observablehq.com/@mattdzugan/population-by-time-zone-creating-a-dataset viewof sortParams = Inputs.form([ Inputs.toggle({ label: "Sort ascending" }), Inputs.toggle({ label: "Sort by offset" }), ]) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: timezonepopstackedbar //| class: stackedbar // https://observablehq.com/@mattdzugan/population-by-time-zone-creating-a-dataset { await whenVisible("timezonepopstackedbar"); return Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1000), height: 100 + Math.min(width / 25, 20), marginBottom: 50, style: `overflow: visible;font-size:${15 + Math.min(width / 90, 11)}px;`, color: {scheme: "RdBu", className: "barPlotLegend"}, marginLeft: 80 + Math.min(width / 100, 20), y: { label: null }, x: { grid: true, label: "Population (billions)", labelOffset: 45 + Math.min(width / 90, 22), transform: d => d / 1e9 }, marks: [ Plot.barX(sortedPop, {x: "pop", y: "Sign", fill: "Offset", stroke: "black", tip: true }), ] }); } ``` Negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets only exist in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas#:~:text=a%20landmass%20comprising%20the%20totality%20of%20North%20America%20and%20South%20America) and islands in the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Atlantic_Ocean) and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean) Oceans. Therefore, the bar chart above is essentially comparing the populations of the Americas and the rest of the world. According to 2021 [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs#:~:text=part%20of%20the%20United%20Nations%20Secretariat) data, roughly 1 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Americas. Dec forbids the association of dates with negative offsets. Therefore, Dec will add ten [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to any negative offset and add one day to the date associated with that offset. Negative offset handling has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or the conversion of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and is typically only necessary after a "year month day" ([ymd](#ymd){#yearmonthday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"}) triplet is converted into a Dec date. If we do know whether Day [364]{.color364by365} belongs to a common or leap year, adding one day to it yields either Day [0]{.color0} or Day [365]{.color365by366} and this uncertainty is expressed as a [multiplication sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication_sign) over the last digit of [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0}. The sign hints that [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is short for [365]{.color0}×`leap`, where [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is either [365]{.color365by366} if `leap` is 1 or [0]{.color0} if `leap` is 0. We can find `leap` by passing any year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}) to @eq-leap below. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07} $$ \text{leap}=\begin{cases} 1&{\begin{aligned} &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\ &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 100\neq0\\ &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\ 0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases} $$ {#eq-leap} ::: # Day of week {#sec-dow .hiddenheading} Adding one day to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, but it increments the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} and "day of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). Dec meets the expectations of [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20currently%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) users who live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with negative offsets by essentially deriving the previous [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} or [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} from the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} if a location in the Americas is provided without an offset or with a negative offset. # Time zone offset {#sec-tzo .hiddenheading} In Dec, "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) are derived solely from longitude. Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}), arcbeats ([a](#a){#arcbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}), or submultiples thereof. If we travel East or West until we reach our starting point, we will cover 1 [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal line on a map"} or 100000 ([10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"}) [a](#a){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}. A [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} is essentially a [deciwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a wěi"} ([dw](#dw){#deciwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}) longitude that became a single-digit [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} integer via [truncation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncation#Truncation_and_floor_function:~:text=truncation%20is%20limiting%20the%20number%20of%20digits%20right%20of%20the%20decimal%20point) or [flooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=takes%20as%20input%20a%20real%20number%20x%2C%20and%20gives%20as%20output%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x): ⌊\${longInputHsl} ÷ 100⌋ = \${longFloorHsl}. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: loninput //| class: slider viewof lonInput = Inputs.range([0, 999], {label: "Milliwěi", value: 500, step: 1}) ``` The [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is approximately ([~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}) 1 [taur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="circumference = 𝜏r"} ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"} [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) long. Near the Equator, a longitude that has a [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_degrees#Precision) of 0.1 [microwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of wěi"} ([µw](#uw){#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microwěi"}) or 10 milliarcbeats ([ma](#ma){#milliarcbeats .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}) is accurate to within [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.1 [microtaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of taur"} ([µc](#uc){#microtaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microtaur"}), [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}10 "zone equatorial meters" ([zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), or 4 [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre#Definition:~:text=the%20base%20unit%20of%20length%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units), which is about the width of a [U-shaped living room layout](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/living-room-layouts) or the length of a typical [subcompact car](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/subcompact-cars-b-segment). For precise [geopositioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopositioning#:~:text=estimating%20the%20geographic%20position%20of%20an%20object%20or%20a%20person), we may want to express [geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) in [ma](#ma){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}, but we are unlikely to need [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} when displaying the [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) or estimates of what the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will be when the Sun rises, reaches its [highest point of the day](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon), or sets. By default, Dec uses [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} precision to display a solar time and the "solar time offset" ([sto](#sto){#solartimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}) used to produce it. # Solar time offset {#sec-sto .hiddenheading} Dec never forces anyone to change their offset and therefore has nothing like [daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time). In Dec, any offset can be referred to as a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}, even if it is not used to match solar time, but there are only 10 [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, because there are only 10 Dec time zones. Dec translates [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to Zone [0]{.color0} and UTC−12:00 or UTC+12:00 to Zone [5]{.color5}, but all other [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets are considered [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offsets"} and not [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}. Anyone can use any offset at any time, as long as they provide the offset after the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. A Dec time is [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}−offset, just like a [Dec date](/dec/date) is year+day. For example, when I wrote this paragraph, my Dec date was 2026+242 and my Dec time was .520−[8]{.color8}. Like Dec dates, Dec times are truncated math expressions. When we evaluate the expression represented by a Dec time, we get a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, as shown in @eq-zone0tod. Unlike a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, which can be written without a dot in the unit of its last digit, an offset never has a dot but is always read as if it were preceded by one, so its first digit is in [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}. The offset [8]{.color8} is 0.8 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, and 700−[8]{.color8} is the same time as 900−[0]{.color0}. If my current time is .520−[8]{.color8}, the time in Zone [0]{.color0} is .720−[0]{.color0}: (.520 − 0.8) mod 1 = .720. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup08} $$\text{zone0tod} = (\text{tod} - .\text{offset}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-zone0tod} ::: The default offset is like a user preference that Dec can remember and update as needed. If a user does not select a default offset, Dec will try to infer their default offset from their longitude, and if offset inference fails, the final fallback is a default offset of [0]{.color0}. If someone wants to change their default offset for a certain period of time, Dec supports automatic offset changes based on user instructions. Users can share automatic offset changes, but they have to opt in to any change to their default offset instead of opting out of a required change. The [Dec span](/dec/span) article will describe automatic offset changes in more detail. A default offset can have up to six digits that mix [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} as desired. This flexibility is meant to support scientific and technical purposes, so users are advised to choose one of the ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, which requires only one [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digit. Dec may simplify the selected default offset. For example, [α]{.color0} and [☉]{.color0} are the same as [0]{.color0}, and there is not much point in displaying [α]{.color0} or [☉]{.color0} when [0]{.color0} is easier to understand. Dec stores the default offset as both a string and a decimal number. The string is displayed to the user and the decimal number is used to adjust the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. Swatch Internet Time, for instance, would be displayed as [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}−[β]{.color1by24}, because its time zone is 1 hour or 1/24 of a day ahead of Zone [0]{.color0}. China is a good example of the difference between a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}. The territory of China spans three Dec time zones, Zones [2]{.color2}, [3]{.color3}, and [4]{.color4}, but the government of China has decided that everyone in China should use UTC+08:00, which is Earth ([♁]{.color3by9}) in [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} or iota ([ι]{.color8by24}) in [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Dec does not enforce the use of any offset, but it would suggest that users in China consider a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} of [3]{.color3} [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}, which is not far off from 8/24, 1/3, [♁]{.color3by9}, or [ι]{.color8by24}. Zone [3]{.color3} may actually be closer to the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of most people in China, because the center of Zone [3]{.color3}, 350 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, is close to the geographic center of China, [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}337 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, whereas the central longitude of UTC+08:00, [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}383 [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}, is much further East. To get a local solar time, we add a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} to a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. If the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} accounts only for longitude, the result is an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}. If it also includes the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}, the result is an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}. Whereas a Dec time zone spans a [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}, a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} represents a single longitude. In @eq-mst below, the [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of a longitude in [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} is (0.95 + [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}) mod 1. # Equation of time {#sec-eot .hiddenheading} The two types of [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) are ["mean solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Mean_solar_time:~:text=it%20follows%20an%20imaginary%20%22mean%20Sun%22%20that%20moves%20along%20the%20celestial%20equator%20at%20a%20constant%20rate%20that%20matches%20the%20real%20Sun%27s%20average%20rate%20over%20the%20year) ([mst](#mst){#meansolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}) and ["apparent solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Apparent_solar_time:~:text=the%20apparent%20motion%20of%20the%20actual%20Sun) ([ast](#ast){#apparentsolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}). To calculate an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, we keep only the decimal part of the sum of 0.95, the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} measured in days, and a longitude measured in [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}. If we want [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} instead of [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, the sum needs to include the result of plugging the "time of year" ([toy](#toy){#timeofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}) into the ["equation of time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_time#:~:text=the%20discrepancy%20between%20two%20kinds%20of%20solar%20time) ([eot](#eot){#equationoftime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09} $$\text{syl} = \text{leap} + 365$$ {#eq-syl} $$\text{toy} = \text{ada} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toy} $$\text{mst} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-mst} $$\text{ast} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w} + \text{eot}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-ast} ::: To obtain a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}, we divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} by a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which is the number of days in the year. Dec passes the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} directly from @eq-toy to the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} function in @eq-eot without first multiplying it by 2𝜋 or 𝜏 to convert it from [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}) to [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}) because the [sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20side%20opposite%20that%20angle%20to%20the%20length%20of%20the%20longest%20side%20of%20the%20triangle) and [cos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20adjacent%20leg%20to%20that%20of%20the%20hypotenuse) [trigonometric Dec are designed for [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10} return plot; } ``` In the [line📈chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_chart#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20chart%20that%20displays%20information%20as%20a%20series%20of%20data%20points%20called%20%27markers%27%20connected%20by%20straight%20line%20segments) above, the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values range from -9.8 to 11.4 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} and the range of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [-365]{.color0} to [365]{.color365by366}, represents a common year followed by a leap year. The [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} reaches about one [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredth of a day"} ([cd]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}) on Days [245]{.color245by365} and [349]{.color349by365}, but passes through zero on Days [45]{.color045by365}, [103]{.color103by365}, [184]{.color184by365}, and [299]{.color299by365}. Therefore, [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} are equivalent four times per year. Apart from transforming an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} into an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, we can also use [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values to more accurately estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow), sunrise, and sunset. @eq-solarnoon below creates a [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow) [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by keeping only the decimal part of the result of subtracting a [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} longitude and an [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} value that is measured in days from the sum of 9.55 and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} that is measured in days. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11} $$\text{solarnoon} = \left(9.55 + \text{tzo} - \text{w} - \text{eot}\right) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-solarnoon} ::: # Cambridge and Cambridge {#sec-cac .hiddenheading} To compare the solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in two cities, we can plug the longitude of each city into @eq-solarnoon above. If all of the variables other than longitude in @eq-solarnoon are set to zero, the resulting solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is almost five [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge#:~:text=a%20city%20and%20non%2Dmetropolitan%20district%20in%20the%20county%20of%20Cambridgeshire%2C%20England) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom#:~:text=a%20country%20in%20Northwestern%20Europe) and nearly seven [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts#:~:text=a%20city%20in%20Middlesex%20County%2C%20Massachusetts%2C%20United%20States) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States#:~:text=a%20country%20primarily%20located%20in%20North%20America). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12} $$4.99635 = (9.55 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk} $$6.97517 = (9.55 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema} ::: The two homonymous cities are about two [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} apart and therefore will always differ by around two [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} in solar time, regardless of what time zone we use as our frame of reference. England is in Zone [0]{.color0} and Massachusetts is in Zone [8]{.color8}. From the perspective of Zone [8]{.color8}, solar noon is roughly [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [5]{.color5} in Cambridge, MA and about [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [3]{.color3} in Cambridge, UK. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13} $$2.99635 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk8} $$4.97517 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema8} ::: # Light arc whole {#sec-law .hiddenheading} The path in the sky that the Sun appears to follow from a sunrise to a sunset is a "light [arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_path#:~:text=arc%2Dlike%20path%20that%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20follow%20across%20the%20sky) whole" ([law](#law){#lightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}). Solar noon, the midpoint of a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}, is halfway between sunrise and sunset. A [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} can be evenly split into two "light arc halves" ([lah](#lah){#lightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"}). Whereas [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} are time points, [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc wholes"} and [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc halves"} are durations. The difference between a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} is a sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14} $$\text{law} = \text{lah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-law} $$\begin{split} \text{sunrise} & = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} \\ & = \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} \\ & = \text{sunset} - \text{law} \end{split}$$ {#eq-sunrise} $$\begin{split} \text{sunset} & = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} + \text{law} \\ & = \text{sunrise} + \text{law} \\ & = \text{solarnoon} + \text{lah} \\ \end{split}$$ {#eq-sunset} ::: ## Night arc whole {#sec-naw .unnumbered .hiddenheading} The Sun continues its path after it disappears below the horizon, moving from sunset to sunrise along a "night arc whole" ([naw](#naw){#nightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"}). Like [conjugate angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=conjugate%20angles%20sum%20to%20a%20full%20angle), a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} form a full circle that represents one day. Likewise, a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} and a "night arc half" ([nah](#nah){#nightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc half"}) are like two [supplementary angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=sum%20to%20a%20straight%20angle) that form a semicircle from solar noon to the [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} midpoint: [solar midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight#:~:text=the%20time%20opposite%20to%20solar%20noon%2C%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20closest%20to%20the%20nadir%2C%20and%20the%20night%20is%20equidistant%20from%20dusk%20and%20dawn). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15} $$\text{naw} = \text{nah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-naw} $$\begin{split} \text{day} & = \text{law} + \text{naw} \\ & = (\text{lah} + \text{nah}) \ast 2 \end{split}$$ {#eq-day} $$\begin{split} \text{solarmidnight} &= \text{sunrise} - \text{nah} \\ &= \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} - \text{nah} \\ &= \text{sunset} - \text{law} - \text{nah} \end{split}$$ {#eq-solarmidnight} ::: The range input below controls the yellow [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and the blue [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} in the diagram beneath it. At the Equator, the sun always rises about a quarter turn from North and sets around three quarter turns from North, resulting in a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of roughly half a day: 75% − 25% = 50%. If the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is zero, a [polar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_night#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20below%20the%20horizon%20for%20more%20than%2024%C2%A0hours) occurs. A day without a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} is called a [polar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20visible%20at%20the%20local%20midnight). ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: dayarcradio //| className: radiobuttons viewof dayArcSouth = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Northern", false], ["Southern", true]]), {label: "Hemisphere", value: false}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: dayarcinput //| class: slider viewof dayArcInput = Inputs.range([0, 1000], {label: "Light arc whole", value: 375, step: 1}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: dayarcdiagram { await whenVisible("dayarcdiagram"); const svg = d3.create("svg") .attr("width", width) .attr("height", daheight); svg.append("circle") .attr("stroke", window.darkmode ? At solar noon, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is 0 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20%28hemisphere%29%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20south%20of%20the%20equator) and 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator). The [radio](https://observablehq.github.io/framework/inputs/radio#:~:text=allows%20the%20user%20to%20choose%20one%20of%20a%20given%20set%20of%20values)📻input above controls whether the midpoint of the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is 0 or 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}. To measure the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} during the [daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location), point a compass🧭at the spot on the horizon below the Sun. During an [equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator) at the Equator, the Sun goes from East to West directly overhead, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} flips like a switch from 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} to 0.75 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} at solar noon, the "[solar elevation angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_zenith_angle#Summary_of_special_angles:~:text=For%20example%2C%20the-,solar,-elevation%20angle%20is)" ([sea](#sea){#solarelevationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}) peaks at 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}, and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} is 0.5 − sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) × (0.25 − [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}). To obtain the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, we can use the height (h) of a vertical rod on a level surface and the length (L) of its shadow: [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} = atan2(h, L). In addition to determining the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, the [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) function can also be used to calculate [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, as shown in @eq-astjing, where [j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is a latitude measured in turns called [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}). In Dec, [inverse trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions#:~:text=obtain%20an%20angle%20from%20any%20of%20the%20angle%27s%20trigonometric%20ratios) functions like [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) yield [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} as opposed to [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. At the Equator ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0), the latitude is zero and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 + atan2(-sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"})cos([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}), sin([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"})). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16} $$ \text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{atan2}\!\!\left( \begin{aligned} & \text{-sin(saa)cos(sea),} \\ & \text{sin(sea)cos(j) } - \\ & \text{cos(saa)cos(sea)sin(j)} \end{aligned} \right) $$ {#eq-astjing} $$ \text{ast} = \begin{cases} \text{saa} & \text{j} = 0.25 \\ \text{atan2(-sin(saa)cos(sea), sin(sea))} & \text{j} = 0 \\ (1.5 - \text{saa}) \bmod 1 & \text{j} = -0.25 \end{cases} $$ {#eq-extremes} ::: At the North Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0.25), the latitude is 0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. At the South Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = -0.25), the latitude is -0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 − [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} before solar noon or [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 1.5 − [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} after solar noon. In between the Equator and the South or North Pole (-0.25 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0 ∨ 0 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0.25), we should use Equation -@eq-ast, -@eq-astjing, or -@eq-astsha. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17} $$ \text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{arccos}\!\!\left(\dfrac{\text{sin(sea)} - \text{sin(j)sin(sda)}}{\text{cos(j)cos(sda)}}\right) \ast \begin{cases} \text{-}1 & 0 \le \text{saa} < 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5 \le \text{saa} < 1 \end{cases} $$ {#eq-astsha} ::: Unlike @eq-astjing, @eq-astsha requires a "solar declination angle" ([sda](#sda){#solardeclinationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}). Whereas latitude is the angle from the Equator in the [geographic coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20spherical%20or%20geodetic%20coordinate%20system%20for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude), [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination#:~:text=the%20angular%20distance%20from%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere) is the angle from the [celestial equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_equator) in the [equatorial coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20celestial%20coordinate%20system%20widely%20used%20to%20specify%20the%20positions%20of%20celestial%20objects). For simplicity, we can use @eq-eot for both the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. The line plot below shows [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angles"} over the course of a year. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: sdaplot // https://observablehq.com/@mcmcclur/plot-for-mathematicians { await whenVisible("sdaplot"); From the northward to the southward equinox, the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is positive and every latitude in the Northern Hemisphere has a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} that is longer than the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} at the Equator, whereas every latitude in the Southern Hemisphere has a shorter one. This pattern is reversed when the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is negative.
