Nearly 7 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Northern Hemisphere and thus experience the longest [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of the year at the [northern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_solstice#:~:text=In%20the%20Northern%20Hemisphere%2C%20the%20June%20solstice%20is%20the%20summer%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20longest%20period%20of%20daylight%29%2C%20while%20in%20the%20Southern%20Hemisphere%20it%20is%20the%20winter%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20shortest%20period%20of%20daylight%29). ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: hemipoptoggles //| class: togs // https://observablehq.com/@mattdzugan/population-by-time-zone-creating-a-dataset viewof sortParamsHemi = Inputs.form([ Inputs.toggle({ label: "Sort ascending" }), Inputs.toggle({ label: "Sort by offset" }), ]) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: hemipopstackedbar //| class: stackedbar { await whenVisible("hemipopstackedbar"); return Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1000), height: 100 + Math.min(width / 25, 20), marginBottom: 50, style: `overflow: visible;font-size:${15 + Math.min(width / 90, 11)}px;`, color: {scheme: "RdBu", className: "barPlotLegend"}, marginLeft: 90 + Math.min(width / 100, 20), y: { label: null }, x: { grid: true, label: "Population (billions)", labelOffset: 40 + Math.min(width / 90, 22), transform: d => d}, marks: [ Plot.barX(sortedPopHemi, {x: "Population", y: "Hemisphere", fill: "Offset", stroke: "black", tip: true }), ] }); } ``` The top range input below picks the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that we will convert into a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} and then pass to our [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model. The two range inputs beneath the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input choose the geographic coordinates needed to find the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}. While the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} rely on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and both geographic coordinates, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} depends on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and latitude but not on longitude. The default latitude, 118 [mj](#mj){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}, is that of Cambridge, Massachusetts. At the Equator, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is about 0.505 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} all year long, so the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input changes the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} only away from the Equator: \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} − \${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: doyinput //| class: slider viewof doyInput = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day of year", value: 183, step: 1}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: latinput //| class: slider viewof latInput = Inputs.range([-250, 250], {label: "Latitude", value: 118, step: 1}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: loninput1 //| class: slider Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 1000], {step: 1, label: "Longitude"}), viewof lonInput) ``` The equation above can be summarized as sunset − sunrise = [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} or [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted) − [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted) = [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference). If we replace the minuend (sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}) with the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the subtrahend (sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}) with the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, the difference will no longer be the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} but rather the time until sunset if it is negative or since sunset if it is positive: \${selectedCurrent.toFixed(3)} = \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} [${selectedDifference < 0 ? "-" : "+"}]{.mono} \${parseFloat(Math.abs(selectedDifference).toFixed(3))}. In general, the subtrahend is the time of an event such as a rocket🚀launch and the difference is the negative [remaining time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event) if the minuend is less than the subtrahend or the positive [elapsed time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Elapsed_Time) if the minuend is greater than the subtrahend. When the minuend is the current time, the difference acts as a ["T minus (T−) countdown"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining) or ["T plus (T+) countup"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=After%20a%20launch%2C%20most%20countdown%20clocks%20begin%20to%20show%20Mission%20Elapsed%20Time). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18} $$\begin{cases}\text{difference}<0&{\text{if } \text{minuend} < \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}=0&{\text{if minuend} = \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}>0&{\text{if minuend}>\text{subtrahend.}}\end{cases}$$ {#eq-difference} ::: Dec uses the term "minuend expansion" to describe the replacement of a minuend with a subtrahend and a difference. We can replace the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the sum of either zero and a "positive interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([pit](#pit){#positiveintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"}), which is the time since the start of the current day (the previous midnight), or 1 day ([d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}) and a "negative interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([nit](#nit){#negativeintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}), which is the negative of the time until the start of the next day (the next midnight), as shown in @eq-todexpansion below. At [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [7]{.color7}, the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} are both 0.7 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and the [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} is -0.3 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}: 0.7 = 0 + 0.7 = 1 + (-0.3). Likewise, a "positive interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([pia](#pia){#positiveintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"}) is the time since the start of the current year and a "negative interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([nia](#nia){#negativeintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"}) is the time until the start of the next year. A [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} equals the current [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}, and a [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"} is the [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} minus the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}, just as a "negative integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) is a "positive integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}) minus the [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}. @eq-adaexpansion applies minuend expansion to the [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup19} $$\text{tod} = 0 + \text{pit} = 1 + \text{nit}$$ {#eq-todexpansion} $$\text{ada} = 0 + \text{pia} = \text{syl} + \text{nia}$$ {#eq-adaexpansion} ::: Dec is not the first system to use [decimal time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#France). During the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution), decimal time was mandatory for French public records for 197 days ([d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}), from [1794]{.color94by100}+[205]{.color205by365} to [1795]{.color95by100}+[037]{.color037by365}. On [1998]{.color98by100}+[247]{.color247by365}, the Swatch corporation announced [Swatch Internet Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Internet_Time), which divides the day into 1000 ".beats", only has one time zone, and is displayed by Dec as [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}−β. Declock measures time in fractional days. A single decimal [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} replaces the three parts of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet and can be shown at any precision by changing its metric prefix. With one [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit and one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit after four [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can match any [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet exactly, and a [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"} keeps Dec in step with [ut](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} without leap seconds. Dec derives its ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} from longitude and never uses negative offsets, but it lets anyone write any [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} after a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} without forcing them to change it. With the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}, we can turn a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into solar time and estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of sunrise, solar noon, and sunset. Finally, minuend expansion turns any [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into a countdown or countup relative to an event, such as midnight, sunset, or the start of the year. # Next {#next .unnumbered} The next article in the [Dec section](/dec) of my [site](/) shows how we can combine [Dec dates](/dec/date) and times into [Dec snaps](/dec/snap)🫰, which are analogous to the [combined date and time representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Combined_date_and_time_representations) in the [ISO 8601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#:~:text=an%20international%20standard%20covering%20the%20worldwide%20exchange%20and%20communication%20of%20date%20and%20time%2Drelated%20data) international standard for dates and times.
